messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Nisha Patel was 45 when she was hospitalized with a sudden, life-threatening respiratory illness that progressed faster than she had understood was possible. Before that, she had been proud of her stamina. As a plumber, she worked in crawl spaces, carried heavy equipment up apartment stairs, and was used to treating her body as dependable and strong. The worst moments of the illness stayed with her in fragments of physical terror: the antiseptic smell that clung to the emergency department curtains, the sharp lightheadedness when she tried to sit upright, and the panicked conviction that each breath might be the one that failed. She remembered lying in a hospital bed trying to pull air in deeply enough, while staff moved around her briskly, and feeling that her own body had turned without warning into something dangerous and unknowable.

In the months after she recovered medically, those sensations did not feel like memories so much as warnings. If she became dizzy on a hot day at work, even for a moment after kneeling under a sink and standing too quickly, she was immediately back in that hospital fear, certain she had to be especially careful because disaster could come out of nowhere. When she caught the antiseptic smell in a clinic hallway or even from cleaning products in a commercial building, her mind went straight to the time she could not breathe and thought she might die. Shortness of breath was especially potent. Climbing stairs with her tool bag or working in a cramped basement could make her chest feel tight, and what frightened her most was not just the sensation itself but what it seemed to prove: that she could no longer trust her own body. These moments left her feeling on guard, scanning herself closely, convinced that if she let her attention slip, she would miss the next sign of catastrophe.

Over time, Nisha built her life around trying not to stir up that sense of danger. She had come to believe that no one else would protect her in time if something went wrong, and that relying on other people was naive when her illness had struck so abruptly. From that position, avoiding anything medically related came to feel like common sense rather than fear. She delayed routine appointments and ignored reminders for physical exams because hospitals, waiting rooms, and the smell of antiseptic felt intolerable. She would not drive past the emergency entrance of the medical center where she had been treated if there was another route. She also stopped seeking help even when she was worried, telling herself that entering those spaces would only make her worse and that she had to manage on her own. At work she began turning down jobs that involved hauling a water heater, working in overheated utility rooms, or climbing multiple flights with equipment, because any physical strain that left her winded felt like gambling with a body she no longer trusted.

These habits narrowed her life and, in ways that troubled her, seemed to confirm the beliefs she was already living by. Because she avoided exertion, even ordinary physical demands now felt more threatening to her, which she took as further evidence that her body was unreliable. Because she stayed away from doctors and handled her fears privately, she felt increasingly alone with them, more certain that she could not count on others and had to remain constantly vigilant. Her work changed in concrete ways. Nisha had once been the plumber coworkers called for the toughest jobs; now she traded those assignments away, choosing smaller repairs where she could keep herself from getting too breathless. She watched clients and coworkers carefully for signs that they noticed the change. Being single, she was used to managing life independently, but recently that independence had hardened into a rule that she must never let herself be vulnerable.

By the time she sought treatment, the loop had become difficult for her to ignore. A brief episode of dizziness on a job in a poorly ventilated laundry room had led her to sit in her van for nearly an hour, too frightened to return inside and equally unwilling to go to urgent care. She was shaken by how quickly her mind had gone back to the hospital and how certain she had felt that something fatal was beginning again. What finally brought her in was not a wish to talk about the illness for its own sake, but fear about what her life was becoming: a careful, constricted routine organized around never feeling dizzy, never getting out of breath, never smelling anything that reminded her of the hospital. She said she wanted help because she was exhausted from living as if her body might betray her at any moment, and because some part of her still hoped she could work, breathe, and move through the world without feeling that danger was always one step away.
